## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no results yet. With the default recipe, the budget is only about 131k environment steps, or 32 PPO updates of 4,096 samples. That is very few policy updates, so sample efficiency and update count probably matter more than network capacity. Every extra FLOP also costs samples. The current head fits the task: max-pooling build heights over a footprint gives the landing layer, and min/max over a per-cell "next missing target layer" can check placements, including overhangs. Two weaknesses stand out. The receptive field is only 5x5, there is no global context in the head, and the pools discard where each cell sits inside the footprint. Plan: (1) a recipe-only change with fewer epochs, more samples and more updates; (2) an architecture-only change at r≈1.25 with a deeper trunk, a global-context broadcast and a footprint-shaped conv in the head; (3) both together, as the best guess. Comparing the three separates the two effects.

### Round 2
All three round-1 trials trained, but no scores are shown, so there is no measured evidence about which direction helps. I'm going on what the task implies. With the default recipe the agent gets only 32 updates, which is very few, so recipes that give more updates (ppo_epochs 2, fewer envs) are a sensible prior. The hard part to perceive is the landing layer: a brick lands one layer above the highest filled cell under its footprint, and it is correct only if the target layer at that height is missing exactly those cells and nothing below gets sealed. The baseline mixes all layers into column features before pooling over the footprint, so it has to learn landing heights implicitly. This round tests one new structural idea: a per-layer head that scores a placement at every layer and uses a learned softmax gate over layers to pick out the landing one. Alongside it, two recipe-only variants of r1c1 test the return horizon/entropy and pure sample diversity.

### Round 3
No scores are visible, so I can't rank the past trials. All six trained without errors. Each one tests a single idea against r1c1 (2 PPO epochs on the baseline network): r2c2 tests a longer return horizon, r2c3 tests max fresh samples with 1 epoch, r1c3 tests the deeper context network, and r2c1 tests the layer-gated head. Designs are random and never run out, and the default budget has only 32 updates, so I expect more fresh samples with fewer epochs to help most. That idea is not confirmed. With two rounds left, I'm using a cover-the-bets plan. (1) Combine the two recipe ideas (1 epoch plus a longer horizon) on the baseline network. If both help on their own, this should be the best recipe. (2) Train the deeper context and footprint-conv network on the 1-epoch recipe, which shows whether more capacity pays when samples are plentiful. (3) Add one cheap self-attention block over the 8x8 cells for board-wide reasoning, also on the 1-epoch recipe. Final selection uses the real scores, so diverse, plausible candidates are the best hedge.

### Round 4
Scores are hidden, so the only evidence is that every trial trained without errors and stayed well inside the caps. Prior expectations still matter. Training designs are random and endless, so fresh data should help generalisation, which favours fewer epochs and more samples. The exact-build bonus comes at the end of the episode, which favours gamma 0.98 and lambda 0.95. The cheapest wins come from recipe changes on the cheap baseline network, because a bigger network costs samples. This is the last round, and all trials compete for selection. So I combine the changes most likely to help into three different candidates. (1) r3c1 with twice as many gradient steps per update, because 1 epoch with 16 minibatches gives only about 1,600 gradient steps in total. (2) The deeper context network on the r3c1 recipe. (3) The baseline at 2 epochs with the long-horizon settings, as a middle point between sample reuse and fresh data.
